clinicalPearls: A benign cystic swelling arising from the head (caput) of the epididymis and containing milky fluid in which spermatozoa can be identified
Typically a painless, smooth, fluctuant lump felt above and behind (posterosuperior to) the testis and clearly separate from it
Transilluminates on examination, helping to distinguish it from a solid mass
Scrotal ultrasound is diagnostic, showing a well-defined anechoic cyst at the epididymal head, often with fine low-level internal echoes from sperm
Distinguished from a simple epididymal cyst mainly by its content (a spermatocele contains sperm) rather than by clinical behaviour, and the two overlap and are often used interchangeably
Most are small and asymptomatic and need only reassurance; large or symptomatic lesions may be treated by surgical excision (spermatocelectomy)
Aspiration and sclerotherapy are alternatives, but recurrence is common and any intervention risks epididymal obstruction and impaired fertility
reference.pathophysiology: A spermatocele forms when an efferent ductule or tubule at the head of the epididymis becomes obstructed and dilates, retaining spermatozoa and epididymal fluid. The resulting cyst is lined by epithelium and filled with a milky fluid in which sperm are present. Because it arises from the sperm-conducting tubules it lies characteristically at the epididymal head, above and behind the testis, and remains separate from the testicular parenchyma. Growth is usually slow, and the lesion is entirely benign with no malignant potential.
additionalInvestigations: Scrotal ultrasound with Doppler to confirm a cystic lesion separate from the testis
Testicular tumour markers (AFP, beta-hCG, LDH) if any solid component is seen
Semen analysis where fertility is a concern before intervention
Clinical follow-up examination for stable, asymptomatic lesions
redFlags: A solid or vascular component on ultrasound
A hard, irregular, or fixed swelling
reference.prognosis: Excellent, as spermatoceles are benign and frequently stable; even after excision the outlook is good, though surgery carries a small risk to epididymal patency and thus fertility.
pitfalls: Operating on small asymptomatic cysts and risking epididymal obstruction and reduced fertility
Assuming all cystic scrotal lesions are benign without ultrasound to exclude a solid mass
Confusing a spermatocele with a hydrocele, which surrounds the testis anteriorly, or with a varicocele
Failing to counsel younger men about fertility implications before spermatocelectomy
management: Reassurance and conservative observation for small, asymptomatic lesions, as they are benign with no malignant potential
Scrotal ultrasound to confirm a cystic lesion separate from the testis and exclude a solid mass
Surgical excision (spermatocelectomy) reserved for large, symptomatic or bothersome lesions
Counsel on the small risk to epididymal patency and fertility from surgery before intervention
Semen analysis where fertility is a concern prior to any operative treatment
Clinical follow-up of stable lesions, with review if the swelling changes or becomes painful
